clue.text: One replaces mate's European connection facility

indicators.note: to replace something is to take its place, so one letter swaps in where another stood

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, the letter that goes out

explanation.surface: Someone's European partner has been swapped for another, as if in a dating service.
explanation.walkthrough: The I takes the place of the final E of WIFE, giving WI-FI.
explanation.definitionFit: Wi-Fi is the wireless network service that lets devices link up to the internet.

clue.text: Indian officer had rival banged up

indicators.note: something banged up has been knocked about and battered out of shape

explanation.surface: An officer in India has had his rival thrown into jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banged up' is British slang for imprisoned, which suits the surface, but here it means knocked about.
explanation.definitionFit: A havildar was a sergeant-rank non-commissioned soldier in the Indian army.

clue.text: Is a stirrer losing it - and marbles?

indicators.note: losing something means it is no longer there, so those letters drop out

blocks.note: someone who stirs things up agitates
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: Is a troublemaker going mad, losing his marbles?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Losing it' and 'losing one's marbles' both suggest madness, but 'marbles' is the plain definition: agates are a kind of marble.
explanation.definitionFit: Agates are playing marbles, traditionally made of the banded stone of that name.

clue.text: As far as I can tell, it's a book

definitions.text: As far as I can tell

blocks.clueFragment: As far as I can tell
blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: in my opinion
second meaning: a large, heavy volume

explanation.surface: Someone guessing, unsure, that the object in front of them is a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the answer into TO ME, as in 'it seems so to me'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tome is a big scholarly volume, while 'to me' expresses a personal view.

clue.text: Extremely irritating chaser in playground I boxed?

indicators.note: something boxed has been put away inside a case, so a letter goes into a word for one

blocks.note: in the game of tag the child who does the chasing is 'it'
a chest is a box, which holds the letter

explanation.surface: A child, chasing others in the playground, complains of being punched, which is very annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: In tag, the chasing child is called 'it'. 'Boxed' reads as punched in the playground, but it means put in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: The itchiest thing is the one that irritates the skin most, a superlative of itchy.

clue.text: Singer's remix of question one above

definitions.note: the 's is 'is', linking definition to wordplay

indicators.note: a remix of a recording rearranges its parts into a new version

blocks.note: the question a solver might ask about the entry above in the grid, 8 Across: what is a Nina?

explanation.surface: A singer has released a remix of a song posing a question.
explanation.walkthrough: NINA, at 8 Across, sits above this entry; the question 'What is a Nina?' rearranges into SHANIA TWAIN. A nina is a hidden message in a crossword grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Shania Twain is a Canadian country-pop singer famous for 'Man! I Feel Like a Woman!'.

clue.text: Shake, following the morning rounds

indicators.note: coming after something, so the word for a brief moment goes second

blocks.note: a shake, as in 'in two shakes', is a moment, shortened to mo

explanation.surface: A morning routine: a shake following the morning rounds, like a milkman or doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rounds' looks like a doctor's or milkman's morning round, but it means rounds of ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammo is informal for ammunition, and rounds are individual bullets or shells.

clue.text: Out of condition, 10 25 sets this woman an example ...

blocks.note: surface reading: someone unfit, with numbered entries setting an example
setter's reading: the answers to 10 and 25 with the conditional word 'if' taken out spell the singer's surname, and the woman herself is also an example of a hidden grid theme

explanation.surface: Someone out of shape is held up as a cautionary example by a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: SIMI and FONE lose IF ('condition') to leave SIMONE, so this woman is NINA Simone. The ellipsis runs on to 9 Across: a nina is also an example of a ghost theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Nina is a woman's first name, borne by the jazz singer Nina Simone, and also the term for a hidden grid message.

clue.text: ... one here first to greet innkeeper, then nameless writer

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the next word is kept

blocks.note: a writer who will not name himself writes 'the me' as setters write ME for themselves

explanation.surface: Continuing 8 Across: someone here greets a pub landlord and then an anonymous author.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back: a nina is an example of a ghost theme, and there is one here, in this grid, on THE PHANTOM OF THE OPERA.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghost theme is a hidden subject running through a crossword, and this puzzle contains one.

clue.text: It's a double-edged sword, missing the middle of Planet of the Apes

indicators.note: the middle keeps only the central letters of the film's first word
missing means lacking, so those central letters are taken away

blocks.note: the two central letters of the word

explanation.surface: A film review: the movie Planet of the Apes is a double-edged sword, missing a middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Double-edged sword' looks like a figure of speech, but it is literal. 'Of the Apes' is SIMIAN, which drops its AN.
explanation.definitionFit: A simi is a short two-edged sword or knife used in East Africa, notably by the Maasai.

clue.text: 'Jazzed-up' Chinese pro, frequently the chap in the boozer before a show

indicators.note: in places the string of words inside the drinker
before means the drinker comes ahead of the final letter

blocks.note: hep is old jazz slang for hip and lively
the Han are the majority Chinese people
tom is British slang for a prostitute
a toper is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: A lively Chinese professional is a regular in the pub before going to a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boozer' is British slang for a pub, but here it is the drinker. The first five words' letters all sit inside the drinker, just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phantom of the Opera is Andrew Lloyd Webber's long-running stage musical.

clue.text: See 14
Surgery collision cases do one!

indicators.note: cases means encloses, so one word goes round the other

explanation.surface: Hospital cases from a crash: a surgeon tells someone to perform one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do one!' is British slang for go away, not a surgeon's instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rude British commands telling someone to clear off and leave.

clue.text: Fighter's day off? Yes - off work!

indicators.note: off as in gone off or out of order, so these letters are spoilt and rearranged

explanation.surface: A boxer asks whether he has a day off and is told yes, no work today.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'off' is part of the fodder; the second is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Fifty Shades of Grey is E L James's bestselling novel, a written work of fiction.

clue.text: Inspiration for versifier at Olympus?

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Asking what inspired a poet living on the gods' mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate signal: the question mark flags that the whole clue both defines and contains the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Greek Muse of lyric and love poetry, a source of a poet's inspiration.

clue.text: Board that signals agreement from Assemblée Nationale and Bundestag?

blocks.note: French for yes; the Assemblée Nationale is France's parliament
German for yes; the Bundestag is Germany's parliament

explanation.surface: A European committee whose vote shows both French and German parliaments agreeing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' seems to be a committee, but it is the spirit-summoning board whose name joins French and German for yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A Ouija board is a lettered board used in seances to receive supposed messages from spirits.

clue.text: It's solo trip (US-France) it initially managed

definitions.text: It's solo trip (US-France) it initially managed

indicators.note: initially means just the first letter of the word before
managed in the sense of handled and worked into shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A summary of the first solo transatlantic flight, from the US to France, which the aircraft achieved.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: the plane is the 'it' that managed the trip.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spirit of St Louis was Charles Lindbergh's aircraft, flown solo nonstop from New York to Paris in 1927.

clue.text: Second round first, they follow Sun 9th - like our football season?

indicators.note: they follow asks for what comes next after each of the two items named
the second item found goes around the first item found

blocks.note: Monday is the day that follows Sunday

explanation.surface: A fixtures list: matches on Sunday the 9th, describing the British football season.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a cup's second round played first; in fact it gives the order of assembly.
explanation.definitionFit: The English football season runs roughly from August to May, lasting about ten months.

clue.text: See 23
See 6
Following close behind, you stabbed Scarface

indicators.note: a stabbed thing has something driven right into it

blocks.note: Scarface was the nickname of gangster Al Capone

explanation.surface: Someone tailing a notorious gangster stabbed him.
explanation.walkthrough: Scarface was the nickname of Chicago gangster Al Capone; 'you' is the archaic form.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog at heel walks right behind its owner, so the phrase means closely following.

clue.text: Acknowledgement made, say, with difficulty by male?

indicators.note: something done with difficulty comes out awkwardly, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A man struggles to get out an acknowledgement.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark hints at the whole picture: a man replying respectfully to a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'yes, madam' is a polite reply confirming that a lady's instruction has been heard.

clue.text: Commercial for irrigation tool released, shot with inverse black and white film

indicators.note: shot with means streaked through with, so letters run into the words
inverse means the two colours go in the opposite order to the one given

blocks.note: a shadoof is a pole-and-bucket device for raising water

explanation.surface: An advert for a garden hose, shot as a black and white film.
explanation.walkthrough: W goes into SHADOOF and B into OUT, the reverse of the order in which black and white are named.
explanation.definitionFit: Shadow of a Doubt is Alfred Hitchcock's 1943 thriller, shot in monochrome.

clue.text: See 11
Mobile texted fine joke

definitions.note: a phone as spelt in a text message

blocks.note: F is the pencil-lead grade for fine
as in 'have you heard the one about...'

explanation.surface: Someone's mobile phone sends them a nice joke by text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Texted' marks the definition as text-speak spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Fone is the text-message spelling of phone, and a mobile is a cell phone.

clue.text: Henry is at intervals King and, nominally, 11 24

indicators.note: at intervals means only every other letter of the first words is kept

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Henry is, now and then, a king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nominally' means by name: the answer is the name of the title character of 11/24.
explanation.definitionFit: In Gaston Leroux's novel the Phantom of the Opera's real name is Erik.

clue.text: Beggar 24, spending penny, revels

indicators.note: spending a coin means it is gone, so that letter leaves the word

blocks.note: Porgy is the crippled beggar in the opera Porgy and Bess

explanation.surface: A beggar at the opera spends his penny and makes merry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spending a penny' is a British euphemism for going to the toilet, but here P is dropped from PORGY.
explanation.definitionFit: An orgy is a wild party of unrestrained revelry, so the plural noun revels fits.

clue.text: See 14
Retiring to put right skin inflammation

indicators.note: to put something right is to sort it out and rearrange it

explanation.surface: Going to bed to cure a rash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' seems to signal a reversal, but it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Intertrigo is a rash caused by chafing where folds of skin rub together.

clue.text: What immediately follows a power signal

blocks.note: the letter after A in the alphabet, spelt out as a word

explanation.surface: Asking what comes straight after a power signal.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelt-out name of a letter is a common device: BEE is how B is written.
explanation.definitionFit: A beep is a short electronic tone used as an alert or signal.
